I have farmed these lands in Quzhou for over forty years. My wheat went into the ground last October, as it always does — you sow before the cold sets in so the seedlings can establish their roots. Now it is spring, and the wheat is greening up and heading into jointing. I will topdress it with urea when the weather warms, and I will irrigate three more times before harvest in early June: once now at jointing, once at flowering, and once at grain filling. Border irrigation from the well is what we have always done here. I also watch for aphids and powdery mildew — I will spray two or three times if the pests show up, because losing wheat means losing half my year's food and income.

After the wheat comes off in June, I will immediately plant summer maize on the same six mu. There is no time to waste — the maize must mature before autumn frost. I use hybrid seed, Denghai or something similar from the seed shop. I do not till for the maize; I drill the seed directly into the wheat stubble. It saves time, fuel, and keeps moisture in the soil. The maize gets compound fertilizer at sowing and one side-dressing of urea at the V6 stage. I irrigate twice — once after sowing if it is dry, and once at tasseling. Two or three pesticide sprays for corn borers and leaf diseases, and I should harvest around October.

I do not grow cotton or vegetables anymore. At sixty-five, I cannot manage the heavy labor and frequent spraying those crops demand. Wheat and maize are reliable. I eat some of the wheat as flour, sell the rest, and the maize goes to the grain buyer. This rotation has fed my family for generations, and I see no reason to change it.
